review.note: This page is the review gate the brief asks for: a single place where every proposed change, its cost, its risk and the proof it worked sit beside the questions that must be answered before the change is worth making. Four of them have a dated partial or full application from 2026-11-19 (RD-01 fully; RD-03, RD-06 and RD-08 partly), each labelled with what shipped and what still waits on an answer; nothing else is applied. These proposals are filed in their own register and are not duplicated into data/suggestions.json, so no count on any other page moves. Every source link is an official page; where a fact could not be read from an official source it is marked as missing rather than filled in. A second batch (RD-15 to RD-26, filed 2026-11-20 by arena/97ff545d-zone4) feeds the site-design prompt directly — a paste-ready design-prompt v2, question-shaped trendy topic hypotheses under a dated validation rule, cluster architecture, an anti-slop pre-publish gate, a freshness programme, measurement-before-publishing restated as a gate, structured-data hygiene, a disclosed social distribution pack, reader capture, decision receipts, a humanised storefront and an adjacent-niche scorecard — with twelve matching questions (RQ-14 to RQ-25) naming what is known, what is missing, who can supply it and the discovery step. None of these rows is applied.

flow.title: Answer every question, or let the defaults stand
flow.what: Each question records what is already known, what is missing, who can supply it and how to discover it. Where a default exists it is named in the discovery step, so silence is still a recorded decision rather than a gap.

suggestions.title: Give the front page a shopper's headline, not a method statement
suggestions.problem: The hero currently reads “Find the air fryer that fits your counter — with every number fact-checked.” The promise is about the site's checking, not about the reader's dinner. The design register already filed this pattern as anti-slop finding AS-08 (“governance apparatus in the shop window”), and AS-01 records the same habit in article headlines.
suggestions.proposal: Replace the hero H1 and lead with a benefit-first headline and one sentence a shopper would repeat to a friend. Keep a two-line trust row underneath (receipts on every figure / gaps flagged, never hidden) rather than inside the headline. Proposed H1: “Crispy dinners, one counter square.” Proposed lead: “Three air fryers — dual basket, single basket, French-door oven — compared on the numbers their listings state, so you can pick your format in a minute and be sure before you buy.”
suggestions.why: A buyer arriving from search or a link decides in about five seconds whether the page is for them. A headline about the checking method answers a question nobody asked yet; the receipts are the proof, not the pitch.
suggestions.effort: One string pair in scripts/build_site.py plus a rebuild.
suggestions.risk: None to any published product value. The compliance strip and the receipts stay exactly where the gates check them.
suggestions.check: The H1 names a reader outcome; the word “fact-checked” no longer appears in the H1; the disclosure strip still renders above the main content on all pages; scripts/verify.py and qa/audit_site.py stay green.

suggestions.title: Cut navigation from 39 labels to one 9-link primary bar plus a footer directory

Two of the article labels are full questions, so the sidebar is taller than a phone screen. Nothing here breaks a rule, but nothing reads like a shop either.
suggestions.proposal: Primary bar: Home · Shop all · Air fryers · Meat thermometers · Guides · About · Disclosure. The footer keeps a complete four-column directory that reaches literally every page the site publishes, including the governance and decision-support pages this repository exists to show. The disclosure strip stays under the masthead on every page.
suggestions.why: A shopper needs six destinations; a reviewer needs all of them. A single flat list devalues both audiences. The footer directory keeps the existing “every page reachable” rule intact while the primary bar does the selling.
suggestions.effort: Navigation tables and the footer template in scripts/build_site.py; checks in scripts/verify.py follow the new rule.
suggestions.risk: Medium only if a page loses its only inbound link. The build check must assert every published page appears in the footer directory before the label list shrinks.

suggestions.title: Show the product, not a grey box: a photography gate with a clean fallback
suggestions.problem: No product image appears anywhere on the site. Suggestion S-18 and flag F-43 record why: Amazon images are Program Content and may not be copied or hosted here, and generated or stock photography would misrepresent the product. The result is the one thing a shop cannot be — wordless about what the thing looks like.
suggestions.proposal: Build three independent image slots that each fall back to a labelled placeholder: (1) owner-supplied original photography with a written release on file; (2) listing images rendered live by the Amazon link/API on each visitor's click — never downloaded, never cached; (3) an illustrative, clearly-labelled diagram of the listed dimensions drawn from the dimensions already sourced in this repository. Ship the diagram now, because it is the only route that needs no new permission; switch a slot to photography or live listing images when the owner supplies the release or the API access.
suggestions.why: The visual deficit is the largest remaining “looks generated” signal. A dimension diagram is honest, original, and safe, and it answers the counter-space question better than a glossy photo would.
suggestions.effort: Half a day for the diagram generator; minutes to flip a slot on when a release or API access exists.
suggestions.risk: High if any route is shortcuts. Copying listing images breaches the Operating Agreement's Program Content terms (S-18, F-43). Generated imagery of a real product would also breach the accuracy rules.
suggestions.check: No image file in the repository was downloaded from a listing; every placeholder is labelled; the dimension diagram is drawn only from sourced values and is captioned with its source; the build adds the image to the sitemap for image search.
suggestions.shipped_note: The diagram route shipped: scaled footprint diagrams drawn from the listed dimensions appear on the four category tiles and at the top of each category page (docs/imagery.html records every asset). Photographs still need either an owner release or written word from Amazon (RQ-05).

suggestions.title: Publish one buying page worth ranking: the master buying guide
suggestions.problem: Eight articles each cover a slice. There is no single, long, maintained “best air fryer for most kitchens” page — the page shape that both shoppers and search engines treat as the entrance to a buying topic. The current hub is an index of cards, not a guide.
suggestions.proposal: Publish one master buying guide page, maintained in place: the two-format decision in two paragraphs, then a ranked recommendation within verified facts only (D-12 permits ranking inside sourced facts), then a full comparison table, then the five questions people actually ask, each with a two-sentence answer and a link to the deeper guide. Every claim row keeps its listing source.
suggestions.why: One authoritative page absorbs internal links and search interest that eight thin pages split between them. It is also the page a reader would bookmark, which is the behaviour that turns a click into a purchase.
suggestions.effort: One long page assembled from fact rows that already exist; no new verification needed.
suggestions.risk: Any “best” framing must be traceable to a listed field (D-12, D-19). No test result, popularity or price claim may appear.
suggestions.check: Each ranked statement cites a listed field and a source row; no unit conversion; no price, rating or trend claim; the page appears in the sitemap and the feed.

suggestions.title: One weekly editorial item, published on a named day, with the topic chosen from measured questions
suggestions.problem: The current cadence is one guide every 14 days, and the next topic is chosen by editorial instinct because no search data exists yet. A publication that is never seen updating does not earn a returning reader, and a topic queue built on instinct cannot improve.
suggestions.proposal: Publish one item every Tuesday for eight consecutive weeks: four from the existing queue, four seasonal or question-led pieces written from the same fact rows. Record the topic-selection reason for each one in data/publishing.json. Once Search Console is verified (SG-29), the reason field must cite the query that earned the next topic.
suggestions.why: A predictable day is how readers and crawlers learn that the site is alive. The reason field is what turns the calendar from a wish list into a measured loop.
suggestions.effort: One item per week from existing fact rows; the calendar change is a data edit.
suggestions.risk: Cadence commitments that are missed read worse than no cadence. Each item must still carry its fact table and sources; a thin item should slip a week rather than publish.
suggestions.check: data/publishing.json names the day and the eight dates; each published item has a fact table and appears in sitemap.xml and feed.xml; each has a topic-selection reason.

suggestions.title: Annotate every product link with the decision it answers, and add a sticky compare bar on mobile
suggestions.problem: Every product link currently says “View on Amazon” or “Open Amazon link”. A reader who has just read why a format suits them still has to work out which button matches their own case, and on a phone the comparison table is scrolled away by the time they reach the button.
suggestions.proposal: Give each product link a decision label instead of a generic verb: “Best for two dishes at once — see the dual-basket listing”, “Best for a shallow counter — see the single-basket listing”, “Best for hosting — see the 26QT oven”. On mobile, pin a two-button compare bar to the bottom of article pages that returns to the chooser and to the comparison table.
suggestions.why: The label is the last thing a reader reads before leaving the site, so it is the highest-leverage sentence on the page. The sticky bar keeps the decision in reach on the device most readers use.
suggestions.effort: One label field per product and a CSS-only sticky bar; no data change.
suggestions.risk: A label that overstates fit becomes a claim. Each label must repeat a listed field already in the table and must keep rel=“sponsored” and the paid-link label.
suggestions.check: Every shop anchor keeps rel=“sponsored”, the tagged Special Link and the adjacent disclosure; the label text appears in the product comparison table; tap targets are 44px or more on mobile.

suggestions.title: Publish trustworthy structured data for the store pages
suggestions.problem: Only WebSite and Article JSON-LD exist. The product pages carry no ItemList or Product structured data, so a search result cannot show the store as a compared set of listings — and the site has no way to earn the richer result.
suggestions.proposal: Add ItemList structured data to the shop page and the category pages, listing each product by name, ASIN and listing URL exactly as published. Do not emit aggregateRating or offers, because no verified price or rating exists (F-02). Add Article structured data with author and publisher once the About page exists.
suggestions.why: ItemList is the honest structured-data shape for a comparison page. Emitting offers or ratings the site cannot verify would be exactly the kind of markup Google's spam policies treat as misleading.
suggestions.effort: One JSON-LD builder beside the existing website_jsonld().
suggestions.risk: Structured data is machine-readable claims. Any field that is not sourced must be omitted, not estimated.
suggestions.check: The JSON-LD parses; every URL in it is the published tagged Special Link; no offers, no price, no aggregateRating; Google's Rich Results test accepts the ItemList.

suggestions.title: Name the writer and the method on a real About page
suggestions.problem: Anti-slop findings AS-06 and AS-07 record that no page names a person, an organisation or a method. A byline sentence exists, but there is no About page a reader or a crawler can point to when asking “who is behind this and how is it made”.
suggestions.proposal: Publish /about: who runs the site, that the copy is written with automated assistance and then checked field by field against the listing, what the site will not publish (prices, ratings, trend claims), how corrections are handled, and how to report an error. Link it from the footer, from every article byline and from the disclosure strip.
suggestions.why: Authorship is the cheapest trust signal a small site has, and it is the one Google's people-first guidance names first. It also gives the correction path that an affiliate site is expected to have.

suggestions.risk: Low. Claims about how the content is made must match what the repository actually does.

suggestions.title: A visible freshness line, only where a date can be verified
suggestions.problem: The footer says “Data observed 2026-11-14” on every page, including pages that were re-read on 2026-11-19. Freshness is the one signal a small site can honestly beat a big one on, and the site currently rounds it down.
suggestions.proposal: Show a per-record “last read” date taken from the verification records that already exist, plus a short “what changed” line on the product pages. Where a date is missing, show nothing and flag it (F-60 does this for the thermometer records).
suggestions.why: A dated observation is the site's whole editorial premise. Showing the newest verified date is free credibility; showing a stale blanket date is a missed one.
suggestions.effort: One rendering change driven by existing dates in data/products.json and data/verification-session-*.json.
suggestions.risk: Do not invent a date for anything unread. A page with no recorded read date must say so.
suggestions.check: Every date under the freshness line resolves to a dated record in data/; no page shows a date newer than its own verification record.

suggestions.title: One seasonal hub per season, dated and archived
suggestions.problem: The holiday guide exists as a single article. Seasonal traffic arrives on a predictable schedule, and a hub that is rebuilt each season accumulates links and rank instead of starting from zero every year.
suggestions.proposal: Create a seasonal hub page (“Gifts”) that is rewritten each season and kept at one stable URL, with the season and the date stated on the page. Archive the prior season's version under its own dated URL.
suggestions.why: A stable seasonal URL is how a small site compounds a recurring search peak. Dating the season keeps it honest.
suggestions.effort: One template, one hub page per season.
suggestions.risk: Seasonal framing may not become a popularity claim; D-19's dated-snapshot rule applies.
suggestions.check: The hub states its season and date; prior seasons stay reachable; no trend or sales-rank claim appears.

suggestions.title: Rewrite the summary paragraphs so they answer instead of restating
suggestions.problem: Anti-slop finding AS-09 records paragraphs that re-list values the table directly above already states. The reader is told the same number twice and learns nothing the second time.
suggestions.proposal: Where a table already carries a value, replace the paragraph with the judgement the table cannot make: which value matters for which cook, and what it would cost to get it wrong. Delete any sentence whose only content is a number already on the page.
suggestions.why: It is the difference between a listing with commentary and an article. It also shortens every page, which helps the mobile reader.
suggestions.effort: An editorial pass over the eight published articles and the guides; no data change.
suggestions.risk: Judgements must still resolve to a sourced field (D-12); the pass must not introduce a claim without a row.
suggestions.check: No paragraph restates a value already present in the same page's table without adding a judgement; every judgement resolves to a fact row; verify.py stays green.

suggestions.problem: No page carries an image, so no page can appear in image results and every social share is a bare link. The visual deficit is also the strongest “generated” signal left after the copy pass.

Add an Open Graph image generated from the same template so shared links show the comparison.

suggestions.problem: The Suggestions page is 14,210 words, the Decisions page 11,410 and the Flagged page 15,842. Each is a single flat document. A reviewer opening it on a phone has no way to work through it, and a first-time reader has no summary.

suggestions.title: Publish the one page a shopper is actually searching for: a fit-verdict hub with the chooser above the fold
suggestions.problem: The site's pages are strong on method and thin on the page shape a first-time buyer arrives for — “which air fryer fits my kitchen and my cooking”. The comparison page compares and explicitly declines to conclude (anti-slop finding AS-05), the buying guide teaches a five-step method, and the chooser sits below two sections of cards on the landing page. A reader who wants an answer gets a procedure.
suggestions.proposal: Build one hub at /air-fryers-that-fit: the three-question chooser first, then a verdict table with one row per reader situation (two dishes at once; one big dish and a shallow counter; hosting on a deep counter), each row naming the product, the listed fields that justify it, the cash-and-counter cost of the alternative, and a decision-labelled link. Above it, a 40-word answer a reader could quote; below it, the method that produced it. It publishes no price, rating or test result — only listed fields already in the repository — so it needs no new access, only the owner's yes on ranking within verified facts (RQ-11).
suggestions.why: This is the page that earns the click it is optimised for, and it is the page competitors cannot copy without doing the same sourcing. It also gives every existing article a natural internal target.
suggestions.effort: One page assembled from existing fact rows plus the chooser component already built; half a day including the check.
suggestions.risk: Medium. A verdict is a claim, so every line must resolve to a listed field (D-12, D-19). If RQ-11 is answered no, the page can still ship as a situation table with no verdict language.
suggestions.check: Every verdict cell resolves to a fact row with a source link; no price, rating, review count or trend claim appears; the chooser is the first interactive element; the page is in the sitemap, the feed and every article's 'Where next' block.

suggestions.title: Publish trendy, question-shaped topic hypotheses — with a dated validation rule, never a volume claim
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for catchy, trendy articles that earn organic clicks. The repository records ten articles and a ten-topic calendar but zero search-demand evidence, and stating volumes without an authorized export would break the no-fabrication rule.
suggestions.proposal: Adopt these working-title hypotheses — all question-shaped, each tied to a promoted product or category, each filed as HYPOTHESIS until an authorized Search Console export shows impressions: (1) “The ‘24 functions, 7 accessories’ listing — what those numbers can and cannot tell you” (P2); (2) “Air fryer vs. toaster oven vs. dual basket: which one actually saves counter space?” (cluster hub piece); (3) “Instant-read vs. leave-in: what a meat thermometer should tell you” (P4/P5, calendar Wave 3, due 2026-12-01); (4) “The seven numbers to check on any air-fryer listing” (extends the published first-air-fryer checklist); (5) “Air fryer gift guide for small kitchens, 2026” (seasonal, extends the published holiday article); (6) “Why did my listing change? A dated re-check log for shoppers” (freshness angle under D-49). Publish order stays with the calendar; any title earning impressions in the first 28 days keeps its slot, the rest are parked — never padded.
suggestions.why: Catchy is a distribution property: the title must match how a buyer phrases the question. Question-shaped titles are the documented people-first pattern; unverifiable volume claims are how sites become slop.
suggestions.effort: Copy plus calendar entries; each piece ships through the normal verified build and source register.
suggestions.risk: Trend-chasing thin content violates the spam policies; the validation rule exists to park losers early. Honest risk: none of these titles is proven demand — they are hypotheses.
suggestions.check: Every title carries a dated HYPOTHESIS/VALIDATED status in the calendar register; zero invented volume numbers appear anywhere; the first 28-day impression review is logged with its export date.

suggestions.prompt_line: Editorial voice: short, confident, question-shaped headlines a shopper would say out loud; no superlatives without a linked source; every trend claim is dated and labelled HYPOTHESIS until Search Console data says otherwise.

suggestions.title: Declare two topic clusters and link every spoke to its hub with descriptive anchors
suggestions.problem: Articles exist but no page names the cluster structure; readers and crawlers both rely on explicit hub-and-spoke architecture, and the thermometer category has no content spokes yet.
suggestions.proposal: Cluster A — air fryers: hub = docs/articles/air-fryer-buying-guide-2026.html; spokes = the format, capacity, cleanup, feature-name, listing-says and sizes articles plus the four question-led guides. Cluster B — meat thermometers: hub = docs/categories/meat-thermometers.html; spokes = the two Wave-3 guides due 2026-12-01 (T-09/T-10). Each hub gains a “Start here” block listing its spokes in buyer order with descriptive anchors (“How to assess cleanup and counter-space trade-offs”, never “click here”); each spoke links up to its hub once, early, with descriptive text. Markup stays BreadcrumbList (already shipped) plus ItemList (D-53).
suggestions.why: Topical coverage plus honest internal linking is what turns a shelf of articles into an authority on one narrow subject — the documented route to durable rankings.

suggestions.title: Add an anti-slop pre-publish gate every article must pass
suggestions.problem: Google's spam policies and helpful-content guidance both target mass, low-value, interchangeable text — the ‘AI slop’ look — and FTC rules require truthful, non-misleading endorsements. The build checks sources and disclosures but has no named editorial-quality gate.
suggestions.proposal: Add a six-item pass/fail checklist to the article template and to qa/audit_site.py: (1) every factual claim sourced or withheld; (2) at least one first-hand-limit sentence where testing did not happen (“we have not tested this; the figures are the listing's”); (3) the byline states the real role and nothing more; (4) a read-aloud rhythm pass — no list-of-three sentence tics; (5) no superlative without a linked source; (6) the disclosure renders above the article body (qa already checks placement — keep it chained). An article missing any item fails the build and is named in the audit output.
suggestions.why: Conversion comes from trust and differentiation; both are lost when ten articles could have been written about anything.
suggestions.effort: Template plus audit rules; roughly half a day, plus one deliberately broken article to prove the gate fires.
suggestions.risk: Checklist fatigue — keep it to pass/fail; anything softer becomes theatre.
suggestions.check: The seeded broken article is rejected by name; a clean article passes; the audit output lists the six items explicitly.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.prompt_line: Pre-publish gate: source or withhold every claim, state first-hand limits plainly, name the real author, ban unsourced superlatives, keep the disclosure above the article body.

suggestions.title: Freshness programme: dated re-checks, seasonal slots, visible ‘checked on’ lines
suggestions.problem: Freshness is both a ranking-relevant signal for deal-led topics and the only honest answer to ‘is this still true?’, but it currently happens ad hoc and only when a session happens to re-read a listing.
suggestions.proposal: Quarterly listing re-verification via the existing verification-session protocol (title and breadcrumb only — prices, ratings and commission stay withheld per F-02); seasonal front-page slots follow the calendar only (holiday window → January air-fryer reset → thermometer grilling prep in spring), each with its own dated record; articles keep the D-49 date rule and gain a visible “listing re-checked <date>” line drawn from their own records. Stale pieces are refreshed or unpublished — never silently left to age.
suggestions.why: A visible re-check date is the cheapest trust signal available, and it keeps the site's facts from drifting as listings change.
suggestions.effort: Recurring; one session per quarter plus calendar upkeep.
suggestions.risk: Refresh theatre — re-stamping dates without re-reading listings is fabrication; the re-check must remain a recorded read.
suggestions.check: Every seasonal slot and every refreshed article carries a dated record; QA rejects a date with no record behind it.

The endpoint may stay unhosted — tracker.js buffers locally exactly as designed — but no topic choice, headline test or “this is working” claim is made before the export exists.

suggestions.effort: One owner sign-in session plus an export; the agent wires only what is permitted (sitemap, event names, checklist).

suggestions.title: A social distribution pack with disclosure baked into every post
suggestions.problem: The site has an OG/Twitter card and a text-and-shapes social-card pipeline, but no distribution discipline; and an undisclosed affiliate post is an FTC problem, not a growth tactic.
suggestions.proposal: One 1200x630 card per flagship article via the existing make_social_card.sh pipeline (text and shapes, never listing photography); every post carries a plain-language disclosure (“affiliate link — buying through it may earn the site a commission at no extra cost to you”); links that support rel attributes ship rel=sponsored; platforms that strip attributes rely on the verbal disclosure. Cadence follows the publishing calendar; no paid amplification in scope.

suggestions.title: Reader capture: RSS first; email only with explicit consent and an owner-chosen provider
suggestions.problem: The brief's publication path ends at reader capture; the site feeds nobody yet, and an improvised email form would collect PII with no privacy note and no unsubscribe path.
suggestions.proposal: Ship the RSS feed properly (generated already) as the zero-PII channel; if the owner wants email, choose a provider first (RQ-17), publish a privacy note (what is stored, who sees it, how to unsubscribe), disclose the affiliate relationship in every send, and never import or scrape addresses. No popups on the first screen — a quiet “get the next guide” line after the article body only.
suggestions.why: A list compounds; a popup that hides unsubscribe does not. RSS keeps the promise with zero PII at GitHub Pages scale.
suggestions.effort: RSS: done. Email: an owner decision plus provider setup.
suggestions.risk: High if improvised — email is regulated territory; the gate is provider plus privacy note first.
suggestions.check: The feed validates; if email ships, the privacy note is linked from every capture point and the unsubscribe path works from a test send.
suggestions.prompt_line: Reader capture: RSS-first, no popups on screen one, email only with explicit consent, a linked privacy note and working unsubscribe, and FTC-disclosed sends.

suggestions.title: Decision receipts: every accepted proposal records choice, proof and rollback
suggestions.problem: The review gate records decisions in ad-hoc log lines; nothing forces the “how would we know it worked — and when do we undo it?” half of the decision to exist at accept time.
suggestions.proposal: Extend the decisions convention (next build that touches data/decisions.json): when a proposal is accepted, its receipt records the date, the person choosing, the check that ran (copied from the proposal's check field), and a rollback trigger with a 28-day review line. The Decision centre renders receipts beside open decisions; rejected rows stay visible with the reason they were rejected.
suggestions.why: Deciding without a receipt is how sites drift into unmeasured “improvements”; receipts make every build answerable to evidence.
suggestions.effort: Register convention plus one rendering block; no new infrastructure.
suggestions.risk: Low; the cost is discipline, not code.
suggestions.check: Every Recorded decision from this batch carries a receipt naming its check and rollback trigger; the Decision centre renders them.

suggestions.prompt_line: Governance: every accepted change ships with a dated receipt — chooser, the check that ran, a rollback trigger, and a 28-day review line.

suggestions.title: Humanise the storefront: a dated editor's note, honest bylines and a corrections log
suggestions.problem: Nothing on the front page says who runs the site or admits error; readers and reviewers both read that absence as “generated”.
suggestions.proposal: Surface a three-line “From the desk” note on the front page (who: the site owner; what it checks: every figure tied to a listing or withheld; what it never does: copy listing photos, invent prices, bury the disclosure); add a dated corrections log page (append-only; its first entry may be “no corrections yet as of 2026-11-20”); bylines stay exactly as honest as the About page — if the owner is the only human, the byline says so.
suggestions.why: Named, fallible, accountable authorship is the oldest answer to “is this a person?” — and the cheapest trust upgrade available.
suggestions.effort: Copy plus one small page through the verified build.
suggestions.risk: Low; the only failure is an invented bio, which the check forbids.
suggestions.check: The front page shows the note; the corrections page exists with a dated entry; no credential appears that the owner has not stated.

suggestions.prompt_line: Human surface: a dated editor's note and a corrections log; bylines claim only what the owner states; nothing generated signs an article.

suggestions.title: Adjacent-niche scorecard before expanding beyond air fryers and thermometers
suggestions.problem: The site has no recorded way to say yes or no to the next niche; growth by enthusiasm is how an air-fryer guide becomes an everything-store with no authority.
suggestions.proposal: Before any new category, fill a scorecard from recorded data only: demand evidence (Search Console once measured; otherwise blank), commission-band reference (the public Table 1 category row only — never a per-ASIN claim), content feasibility (how many question-shaped topics the cluster supports), policy risk (Amazon and FTC fit) and inventory risk (recorded volatility or blank). Cells that cannot be filled stay blank — the scorecard's first use is to kill bad ideas, not to rank them.
suggestions.why: D-46 (thermometers) worked because scope was recorded explicitly and stayed reversible; scaling that habit prevents niche sprawl.
suggestions.effort: One register row-set per candidate niche; one session each.
suggestions.risk: Low; the risk lives in skipping the card, not in using it.
suggestions.check: Each expansion proposal arrives with a filled or explicitly blank scorecard; no forecast totals appear anywhere.
